reconcile.connective: Defenders distinguish senses of "hate": God's love is essential and universal, while his "hatred" of Esau and the wicked is relative rejection and aversion to sin, not personal malice.

discrepancy.connective: Thomas Paine presses the sharpest form of the objection, charging that the vindictive, nation-hating deity of the Hebrew Bible cannot be squared with the benevolent God love is said to describe.

skeptic.name: Thomas Paine
skeptic.attribution: Thomas Paine (d. 1809), The Age of Reason (1794-95)

excerpts.excerpt_text: hated—not positively, but relatively; that is, did not choose him out to be the object of gratuitous favor, as I did Jacob …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly recasts the OT 'hate' language (Esau, picked up in Rom 9:13) as relative non-choosing rather than positive malice, dissolving the conflict with 'God is love.'

excerpts.excerpt_text: by which is meant not positive hatred, which can only have for its object sin and sinners, or persons so considered; but negative hatred, which is God's will, not to give eternal life to some persons …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Explicitly partitions 'hate' into positive vs. negative senses, locating God's hatred in withholding of favor rather than in opposition to his being love.

excerpts.excerpt_text: Not that this is the only conception we ought to have of him; we have found that he is light as well as love …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Qualifies the 'God is love' absolutization the contradiction leans on—he is also light (holiness), which grounds his aversion to the wicked without negating his love.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the love/hate language for Jacob and Esau under the Hebrew idiom of 'loving less,' arguing the term marks preference and rejection rather than the emotion of hatred.

link.title: GotQuestions: Why did God love Jacob and hate Esau (Malachi 1:3; Romans 9:13)?
link.note: live apologetic treatment arguing God's 'hate' is non-selection, not malice, and is compatible with God loving everyone
